title: Features and labels
story:
A table does not arrive divided into the thing you are predicting and the things you are allowed to predict it from. Somebody draws that line, and where they draw it defines the problem rather than describing the data. Two different lines through the same table are two different problems with different answers, and neither is more natural than the other.

Start with the label, because it is the decision people spend least time on. The label should be the thing you will actually act on, and it usually is not the thing that is easiest to obtain. Predicting whether a customer cancelled is easy to label and may be useless if the action you can take is retention outreach, which needs to happen before the cancellation is decided. Predicting whether a transaction was flagged as fraud is not the same as predicting whether it was fraud — one labels the output of your existing detection system, so a model trained on it learns to imitate that system, including everything it currently misses. Ask what decision the prediction feeds, and label the thing that decision turns on.

Then the features, where the constraint is sharper than it looks. The formalisation of leakage defines it as information about the target that should not be legitimately available to mine from, and the crucial word is legitimately: the illegitimate information is usually introduced unintentionally, facilitated by the data collection, aggregation and preparation process. The remedy proposed is a learn-predict separation, and what that makes precise is that legitimacy is a fact about time. A column qualifies if its value was knowable at the moment the prediction must be made. Whether it sits in the table is irrelevant — the table was assembled afterwards, which is exactly why it contains things the prediction moment did not.

There is a second constraint that is easy to miss, and it rules out the obvious workflow. You cannot select features one at a time. Models are described as machines for creating entanglement, which makes the isolation of improvements effectively impossible: changing the input distribution of one feature may alter the importance, weights or use of all the remaining ones, and adding or removing a feature does the same, because no inputs are ever really independent. That is the CACE principle — Changing Anything Changes Everything. So a feature's value is not a property it has; it is a property of the set it is in. Dropping the weakest feature by some importance measure can improve a model, leave it unchanged, or make it worse, and which of those happens is not predictable from the measure.

The practical shape that follows: decide the label from the decision, admit features by when they became knowable, and evaluate feature sets rather than features.

problem.name: Problem framing
problem.shape: A table has to be split into a thing being predicted and things permitted to predict it, and neither side of that split is given by the data.
tell: the label was chosen because it was the easiest column to obtain
the label records the output of a system you are trying to replace
nobody has asked when each feature's value becomes knowable
features are being added or dropped one at a time and judged individually
problem.move: Work backwards from the decision the prediction feeds, and label the thing that decision turns on. Admit a feature only if its value was knowable at the moment of prediction, which is a question about time rather than about the table. Then change feature sets rather than features, and measure end to end.
problem.invariant: Legitimacy is a fact about when a value became knowable, not about whether it appears in the dataset. The table was assembled after the fact, so containing a column is no evidence that the column was available.
problem.breaks: The per-feature question has a clean answer and the per-feature decision does not. Because the parameters are fitted jointly, a feature's contribution depends on which others are present — so admissibility can be settled one column at a time while usefulness cannot be, and an importance ranking does not predict what removal will do.

cost.time: a provenance question per column, and evaluation of sets rather than of individual features, which multiplies the number of runs
cost.beats: taking the table as given, which lets the collection process choose your problem, and ranking features by importance to prune them, which assumes an independence the model does not have

worked.problem: What makes a column a legitimate feature?
worked.reasoning:
That its value was knowable at the moment the prediction has to be made. Not that it is in the table — the table was assembled afterwards.

This is the distinction the formal treatment of leakage rests on: information about the target that should not be legitimately available to mine from, introduced unintentionally and facilitated by the collection, aggregation and preparation process. The remedy is a learn-predict separation, which is really an instruction to reconstruct what was known at prediction time and admit nothing else.

So the test I apply to each column is temporal. Imagine the instant the model must produce its output. Did this value exist then, and would the system have had access to it? Three patterns fail. Values recorded after the outcome — a resolution code, a closure date, a status set downstream. Values aggregated over a window that extends past the prediction point, which is the subtle one, because a feature like average spend over the customer's lifetime silently includes the future. And values that encode how the dataset was assembled rather than what it describes, such as an identifier whose ranges trace which source a row was joined from.

There is a second question that looks similar and is not, and conflating them causes trouble. Admissibility is per-column and has a definite answer. Usefulness is not per-column at all. Because the parameters are fitted jointly, changing one feature's input distribution may alter the importance, weights or use of all the others, and adding or removing a feature does the same, since no inputs are ever really independent — Changing Anything Changes Everything. A feature's contribution is a property of the set it sits in rather than of the feature.

Practically that means I answer admissibility column by column, and never answer usefulness that way. Pruning the lowest-ranked feature by an importance measure is a hypothesis to be tested end to end, not a conclusion the measure supports.

And I would note that the label deserves the same scrutiny. A label recording what an existing system flagged trains a model to imitate that system, including its blind spots, which is a different problem from the one people usually think they are solving.

problem.practice: Take your current label and ask what decision it feeds and when that decision has to be made. Then take your three strongest features and establish, for each, the moment its value became knowable. If any of them is an aggregate, check what window it covers and whether that window ends before the prediction point.

beats.broke: A table does not arrive divided into what you are predicting and what you may predict it from; somebody decides, and the decision defines the problem rather than describing the data.
beats.fix: Choose the label to be the thing you will actually act on, and admit a feature only if its value was knowable at the moment the prediction has to be made.
beats.cost: Both decisions are unverifiable from inside the dataset — legitimacy is a fact about when a value came into existence — and features cannot be chosen one at a time, because adding or removing one changes the role of all the others.

interview.q: What makes a column a legitimate feature?
interview.trap: Answering that it must be correlated with the target and not be the target. The test is temporal rather than semantic: a value that was not knowable when the prediction must be made is inadmissible however innocuous it looks, and a lifetime aggregate can smuggle the future in without any suspicious column appearing.

takeaway: Where you draw the line between label and features defines the problem, and a feature is admissible because of when its value became knowable rather than because of what it contains — while usefulness is never a property of a single feature at all.
